intro: Listen to a Spanish-speaking parent for one evening and count the sentences that are not statements of fact. "Quiero que comas." (I want you to eat.) "Espero que te vaya bien." (I hope it goes well for you.) "No creo que llueva." (I do not think it will rain.) "Si tuviera tiempo, te llevaría." (If I had time, I would take you.) Wishes, hopes, doubts and imagined worlds fill ordinary talk, and Spanish marks every one of them with a change in the verb. That change is the subjunctive mood, and this unit is about learning to hear it, form it, and use it on purpose.

The first chapter starts with a letter of advice from an older sister at college and uses it to answer three questions: what a mood is, how to build the present subjunctive from the yo form, and which words trigger it. You will learn the six irregulars (sea, esté, vaya, haya, sepa, dé), the two-clause pattern with que and a change of subject, and the WEIRDO triggers: wishes, emotions, impersonal expressions, recommendations, doubt and ojalá. The second chapter follows a class writing about one thing they would change in their town. It adds doubt versus certainty, conjunctions like para que and cuando, the imperfect subjunctive built from the preterite, the conditional, and the if-sentence that puts them together: Si tuviera dinero, viajaría.

Many heritage speakers already say these forms without thinking. This unit shows why they work, so you can check your own writing, fix a sentence that sounds off, and explain the rule to someone else. By the end you will write a letter of advice and a paragraph about a change you would make, with every wish, doubt and imagined condition in the right mood.
bigQuestion: How does Spanish use the shape of a verb to separate what is from what someone wants, doubts, feels or imagines?

the indicative — the mood for reporting facts: Mateo estudia

test.q: Which sentence is in the subjunctive mood?
choices: Es importante que duermas ocho horas.
test.why: Es importante que is an impersonal trigger with a new subject, so duermas is subjunctive. The others report in the indicative.

test.q: What is the ustedes present subjunctive of hablar?
test.why: Drop the -o from hablo and add the -ar subjunctive ending -en: hablen.
The subjunctive comes from the yo form tengo, so the tú form is tengas. Tienes is indicative.

test.q: Which is the present subjunctive of ser for nosotros?
test.why: Ser is irregular: sea, seas, sea, seamos. Somos is indicative, fuéramos is imperfect subjunctive, seremos is future.

test.q: Which sentence should use the infinitive?
test.why: With no change of subject, Spanish uses the infinitive: Quiero comer. The others switch to a new subject after que.
Es cierto que reports certainty: Es cierto que hace frío. The other three trigger the subjunctive.

test.q: Which sentence means "Mom tells me to sleep more"?
choices: Mamá me dice que duerma más.
test.why: Decir with a subjunctive clause gives an instruction: me dice que duerma. With duermo it would only report that I sleep more.

test.q: No creo que el autobús ___ (pasar) después de las nueve.
test.why: No creer que expresses doubt, so the verb is the subjunctive pase.

test.q: Arreglan las luces para que la gente ___ (caminar) segura de noche.
test.why: Para que always takes the subjunctive: camine.

test.q: Which cuando sentence describes a habit?
choices: Cuando hace calor, me siento en la sombra.
test.why: Cuando hace calor, me siento describes what happens regularly, so both verbs are present indicative. The others point to the future and take the subjunctive.

test.q: What is the yo imperfect subjunctive of ir?
test.why: From the preterite fueron, drop -ron and add -ra: fuera. Vaya is present subjunctive, iba is imperfect, iría is conditional.

test.q: El maestro pidió que nosotros ___ (escribir) un párrafo.
test.why: A past trigger, pidió, takes the imperfect subjunctive: escribiéramos, with the accent before -ramos.

test.q: What is the yo conditional of poner?
test.why: Poner uses the irregular stem pondr- in the conditional: pondría. Ponía is imperfect, pondré is future, ponga is present subjunctive.

test.q: Si yo ___ (poder) cambiar una cosa, arreglaría el parque.
test.why: An imagined condition after si takes the imperfect subjunctive: pudiera. The conditional belongs in the result clause.

test.q: What does "Si tuviéramos más autobuses, la gente no manejaría tanto" mean?
choices: If we have more buses, people do not drive much.
If we had more buses, people would not drive so much.
We have more buses, so people do not drive.
I hope we have more buses so people drive less.
test.why: Si plus the imperfect subjunctive tuviéramos with the conditional manejaría is a contrary-to-fact if-sentence: if we had, people would not.

write.prompt: Escribe una carta de consejos a un amigo que empieza la escuela secundaria y termina con lo que cambiarías de tu ciudad. Write a short letter in Spanish with two wishes or recommendations (quiero que, te recomiendo que), one doubt or emotion (dudo que, me alegra que), one sentence with para que or cuando, and one si sentence with the imperfect subjunctive and the conditional.

Build each present subjunctive from the yo form and check the opposite vowel: -ar verbs take e, -er and -ir verbs take a.
Check the six irregulars: sea, esté, vaya, haya, sepa, dé.
In the si sentence, keep -ra in the si clause and -ía in the result: Si tuviera…, cambiaría….
Read every sentence aloud with its trigger; if the verb ends in -o after quiero que, fix it.

title: The Subjunctive

chapters.title: What the Subjunctive Is
chapters.bigQuestion: How does Spanish change a verb to show that a sentence wishes, doubts or reacts instead of simply reporting?

story.title: A Letter from Lucía
story.kicker: An older sister writes home from her first month of college, and every piece of advice she gives uses a verb form her brother has never studied.
paragraphs: Mateo is a junior at a high school on the Southwest Side of Chicago. His sister Lucía left in August for her first year at a university downstate. She promised to write a real letter, on paper, once she had settled in. In October it finally arrives. Mateo reads it at the kitchen table while their mother makes coffee, and he notices something strange about the verbs.

"Quiero que estudies un poco cada día, no todo la noche antes del examen," she writes. (I want you to study a little every day, not all of it the night before the exam.) "Es importante que duermas. Te recomiendo que hables con tus maestros cuando no entiendas algo." (It is important that you sleep. I recommend that you talk with your teachers when you do not understand something.) Mateo knows the verb *estudiar*. He knows *tú estudias*. So why does Lucía write *estudies*?

He keeps reading. "Ojalá que vengas a visitarme en noviembre. Espero que mamá esté bien y que no trabaje tanto." (I hope you come visit me in November. I hope Mom is well and does not work so much.) Every hope, every wish, every piece of advice has the same twist: an -ar verb ends in -e, and an -er or -ir verb ends in -a. Lucía is not making mistakes. She is using a form that Spanish saves for exactly this kind of sentence.

That evening Mateo shows the letter to his mother. She reads it twice and smiles. "Así hablo yo contigo," she says. (That is how I talk to you.) "Quiero que comas. Necesito que me ayudes." (I want you to eat. I need you to help me.) He has heard those sentences his whole life. He just never noticed that the verb was doing something different. This chapter is about that difference: the subjunctive mood.

By the end of the chapter, Mateo will be able to write back. He will tell Lucía what he hopes for her, what worries him, and what he recommends, and every verb will land in the right form. So will yours.
story.think: Think of a piece of advice someone older gave you. In English, how do you know it was advice and not a plain statement of fact?

lessons.title: Two Moods for One Verb
lessons.mainIdea: Tense tells when something happens; mood tells how the speaker sees it. The indicative reports, and the subjunctive wishes, doubts or reacts.
reading: You already know several tenses. *Hablo* (I speak) is present. *Hablé* (I spoke) is preterite. *Hablaba* (I used to speak) is imperfect. A tense answers the question when. Spanish verbs carry a second kind of information that English mostly hides: mood. Mood answers a different question: is the speaker reporting a fact, or wishing, doubting, or reacting to something? That second job belongs to the *subjuntivo* (subjunctive).

Compare two sentences from Lucía's letter. "Mateo estudia cada día" (Mateo studies every day) is a report. The speaker is stating what happens. That is the *indicativo* (indicative), the mood you have used in every chapter so far. "Quiero que Mateo estudie cada día" (I want Mateo to study every day) is not a report. Nobody is saying that Mateo studies. Lucía is saying what she wants. The verb changes from *estudia* to *estudie* to mark that shift.

English used to do this too, and a few traces remain. "I suggest that he be on time" uses be instead of is. "If I were you" uses were instead of was. Most English speakers never think about those forms, which is why the Spanish subjunctive feels new. It is not new. It is a whole set of endings that Spanish uses every day, in every conversation where someone hopes, asks, doubts or feels something about what another person does.

Here is the rule to carry through the chapter. The indicative states what is. The subjunctive frames what someone wants, doubts, or feels about what might be. The same verb can appear in either mood, and the ending tells you which one you are hearing.

words.d: mood — the form of a verb that shows whether the speaker reports, wishes, doubts or reacts
the indicative — the mood for stating facts and reporting: Mateo estudia (Mateo studies)
the subjunctive — the mood for wishes, doubts, emotions and advice: Quiero que Mateo estudie (I want Mateo to study)
verb tense — the form that shows when: present, preterite, imperfect, future

look.title: Same Verb, Two Jobs
look.text: Read the pairs aloud. Mi mamá trabaja mucho. (My mom works a lot.) Espero que mi mamá no trabaje tanto. (I hope my mom does not work so much.) Los estudiantes duermen ocho horas. (The students sleep eight hours.) Es importante que los estudiantes duerman ocho horas. (It is important that the students sleep eight hours.) In each pair the first sentence reports. The second one hopes or judges.
look.prompt: For each pair, which sentence could be checked as true or false, and which one cannot? What does that tell you about mood?

check.q: Which sentence is in the indicative mood?
choices: Quiero que Mateo estudie cada día.
Ojalá que Mateo estudie cada día.
Es importante que Mateo estudie cada día.
check.why: Mateo estudia reports what happens. The other three use estudie after a wish, a hope or a judgment, so they are subjunctive.

check.q: What does mood tell you about a verb?
choices: Whether the speaker is reporting, wishing, doubting or reacting
Whether the subject is singular or plural
check.why: Tense answers when. Mood answers how the speaker sees the action: as a fact (indicative) or as a wish, doubt or reaction (subjunctive).

check.q: "Espero que mi hermana esté bien." What does this sentence mean?
choices: I hope my sister is well.
I know my sister is well.
check.why: Espero que (I hope that) introduces a wish, so the verb is the subjunctive esté. The sentence hopes; it does not report.

lessons.title: The Two-Clause Pattern
lessons.mainIdea: The subjunctive almost always appears in a second clause after que, when the subject of that clause is different from the subject of the first.
reading: Look at the shape of a subjunctive sentence. "Quiero que estudies." It has two parts. The first, *quiero* (I want), is a main clause in the indicative. Then comes *que* (that). Then a second clause with a different subject, tú, and the verb in the subjunctive: *estudies*. A *cláusula* (clause) is a group of words with its own subject and verb. Most subjunctive sentences are built from exactly two of them, joined by que.

The change of subject is the key. In "Quiero estudiar" (I want to study), I am the one wanting and I am the one studying. There is one subject, so Spanish uses the *infinitivo* (infinitive), the plain -ar, -er or -ir form. In "Quiero que tú estudies" (I want you to study), I want but you study. Two subjects, two clauses, and the second verb goes into the subjunctive. English hides this with "I want you to study," which is why English speakers often say the wrong thing: "Quiero tú estudiar" is not Spanish.

Try it with Lucía's other sentences. "Espero visitar a Lucía" (I hope to visit Lucía): one subject, infinitive. "Espero que Lucía me visite" (I hope Lucía visits me): two subjects, que, subjunctive. "Necesito dormir" (I need to sleep): one subject. "Necesito que duermas" (I need you to sleep): two subjects. The pattern is the same every time. Main clause, que, new subject, subjunctive verb.

One more thing to notice. The que is not optional in Spanish. English can say "I hope she comes" with no that. Spanish must say "Espero que venga." If you see a verb of wanting or hoping followed by que and a new subject, expect the subjunctive to follow.

words.d: clause — a group of words with its own subject and verb; subjunctive sentences usually have two
that — the word that joins the main clause to the subjunctive clause: Quiero que vengas (I want you to come)
infinitive — the plain -ar, -er or -ir form, used when there is no change of subject: Quiero estudiar (I want to study)
change of subject — when the person in the second clause is not the person in the first, which calls for que plus the subjunctive

look.title: One Subject or Two?
look.text: Mateo texts his cousin: Quiero ir al partido el sábado. (I want to go to the game on Saturday.) His cousin answers: Y yo quiero que tú me compres la entrada. (And I want you to buy me the ticket.) Then his mother adds: Necesito que los dos vuelvan antes de las diez. (I need you both to be back before ten.) Count the subjects in each sentence.
look.prompt: Which sentence has one subject and uses the infinitive? Which two have a change of subject? Rewrite the first one so that Mateo wants his cousin to go.

check.q: Why does "Quiero estudiar" use the infinitive while "Quiero que estudies" uses the subjunctive?
choices: The second sentence is a question.
The second sentence is more polite.
The second sentence has a change of subject: I want, you study.
check.why: One subject takes the infinitive. A new subject after que takes the subjunctive.

check.q: Which sentence is correct Spanish for "I hope you come"?
check.why: Spanish needs que and the subjunctive vengas. Espero tú venir copies English word order, and vienes is the indicative.

check.q: Which sentence should use the infinitive, not the subjunctive?
check.why: Necesito dormir has one subject: I need, I sleep. The others switch to a new subject after que.

lessons.title: Start from the Yo Form
lessons.mainIdea: To form the present subjunctive, take the present-tense yo form, drop the -o, and add the opposite vowel endings: -e for -ar verbs, -a for -er and -ir verbs.
reading: The present subjunctive is built in three steps. Step one: take the present indicative yo form. For *hablar* (to speak) that is hablo. Step two: drop the -o. That leaves habl-. Step three: add the subjunctive endings. For -ar verbs they are -e, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en. So hablar gives hable, hables, hable, hablemos, habléis, hablen. Notice the trade: -ar verbs, whose indicative endings use the vowel a, switch to e in the subjunctive.

For -er and -ir verbs the trade runs the other way. *Comer* (to eat): yo como, drop the -o, com-, add -a, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. That gives coma, comas, coma, comamos, comáis, coman. *Vivir* (to live): vivo, viv-, viva, vivas, viva, vivamos, viváis, vivan. Learners sometimes call this the opposite vowel rule. An -ar verb takes e endings; an -er or -ir verb takes a endings. If you can conjugate the present indicative, you already have every piece you need.

Why start from the yo form and not the infinitive? Because many verbs change in the yo form, and the subjunctive keeps that change in all six persons. *Tener* (to have) has the yo form tengo, so its subjunctive is tenga, tengas, tenga, tengamos, tengáis, tengan. *Hacer* (to do, make) has hago, so haga, hagas, haga. *Decir* (to say) has digo, so diga. *Conocer* (to know a person) has conozco, so conozca. *Salir* (to leave) has salgo, so salga. Start from the infinitive and you would get the wrong stem every time.

Two common mistakes. First, learners forget that the yo and él/ella/usted forms are identical in the subjunctive: hable can mean I speak or he speaks, so context or a subject pronoun tells you which. Second, learners add -o to the subjunctive by habit and write hablo where they mean hable. Say the sentence with the trigger in front of it, Quiero que hable, and the o will sound wrong.

words.d: to conjugate — to change a verb's ending to match its subject and its tense or mood
the yo form — the first-person present form, the starting point for the subjunctive: tengo → tenga
the opposite vowel — -ar verbs take e endings (hable) and -er/-ir verbs take a endings (coma, viva)
the stem — what is left after you drop the ending: habl-, com-, viv-, teng-

look.title: Three Steps, Five Verbs
look.text: Walk through each one. 1. escribir (to write): escribo → escrib- → escriba, escribas, escriba, escribamos, escribáis, escriban. 2. llamar (to call): llamo → llam- → llame, llames, llame, llamemos, llaméis, llamen. 3. poner (to put): pongo → pong- → ponga, pongas, ponga, pongamos, pongáis, pongan. 4. venir (to come): vengo → veng- → venga. 5. ver (to see): veo → ve- → vea, veas, vea, veamos, veáis, vean.
look.prompt: Now do traer (to bring; yo form traigo) and leer (to read; yo form leo) the same way. Which one keeps a surprise from its yo form?

check.q: What is the tú subjunctive form of hablar?
check.why: Drop the -o from hablo and add the -ar subjunctive ending -es: hables. Hablas is indicative, hablarás is future, hablaste is preterite.

check.q: Why is the subjunctive of tener "tenga" and not "tena"?
choices: The subjunctive is built from the yo form tengo, which keeps the g.
check.why: The yo form tengo gives the stem teng-. Every subjunctive form keeps it: tenga, tengas, tengamos.

check.q: Es necesario que nosotros ___ (vivir) cerca de la universidad.
check.why: Vivir is an -ir verb, so it takes the a ending: vivamos. Vivimos is indicative, vivemos is not a form, and vivan is for ellos.

lessons.title: Stem Changes and Spelling Changes
lessons.mainIdea: Stem-changing verbs keep their change in the subjunctive wherever the indicative has it, -ir verbs add a second change in nosotros and vosotros, and -car, -gar and -zar verbs adjust their spelling to keep the sound.
reading: Stem-changing verbs follow the yo-form rule with one extra wrinkle. *Pensar* (to think, e→ie) has the yo form pienso, so the subjunctive is piense, pienses, piense, pensemos, penséis, piensen. The nosotros and vosotros forms drop the change, just as they do in the indicative (pensamos, not piensamos). *Volver* (to return, o→ue) works the same way: vuelva, vuelvas, vuelva, volvamos, volváis, vuelvan. Picture the boot shape you learned for the present tense. It still holds.

Verbs ending in -ir do one more thing. In the nosotros and vosotros forms, where the main change disappears, a smaller change appears: e becomes i, and o becomes u. *Dormir* (to sleep, o→ue) gives duerma, duermas, duerma, durmamos, durmáis, duerman. *Sentir* (to feel, e→ie) gives sienta, sientas, sienta, sintamos, sintáis, sientan. *Pedir* (to ask for, e→i) has the change in every form: pida, pidas, pida, pidamos, pidáis, pidan. Lucía's advice "Es importante que duermas" uses the first one.

The last group is about spelling, not sound. In Spanish, c before e sounds soft, like s, and g before e sounds like the j in jalapeño. When an -ar verb whose stem ends in c, g or z takes the e endings, the spelling has to change to keep the hard sound you hear in the infinitive. *Buscar* (to look for) becomes busque, not busce. *Llegar* (to arrive) becomes llegue, with a silent u to keep the g hard. *Empezar* (to begin, e→ie) becomes empiece, because Spanish does not write z before e.

These are the same three spelling changes you met in the yo form of the preterite: busqué, llegué, empecé. If you remember those, you already know which verbs to watch. A quick test: say the subjunctive form out loud. If the c or g sound has changed from the infinitive, the spelling needs fixing.

words.d: stem change — a vowel change inside the stem: pensar → piense, volver → vuelva, pedir → pida
to sleep — o→ue, with u in nosotros: duerma, duermas, duerma, durmamos, durmáis, duerman
to look for — spelling change c→qu before e: busque, busques, busque
to arrive — spelling change g→gu before e: llegue, llegues, llegue
to begin — e→ie and spelling change z→c before e: empiece, empecemos

look.title: Fixing a Roommate Note
look.text: Lucía's roommate leaves a note in Spanish with three errors. Espero que tú no llegas tarde a la reunión. Es importante que nosotros dormamos bien esta noche. Quiero que la fiesta empieza a las ocho. Each sentence has a trigger (espero que, es importante que, quiero que) and a change of subject, so each second verb should be subjunctive. Llegas should be llegues, dormamos should be durmamos, and empieza should be empiece.
look.prompt: For each fix, name the rule: spelling change, -ir nosotros change, or both stem and spelling change.

check.q: Which is the correct nosotros subjunctive of dormir?
check.why: In -ir stem changers the nosotros form takes the smaller change o→u: durmamos. Duermamos wrongly keeps ue, and dormimos is indicative.

check.q: Quiero que tú ___ (buscar) el libro en la biblioteca.
check.why: The stem ends in c, so before the e ending it becomes qu: busques. Busque is the yo/él form, not tú.

check.q: Why does the subjunctive of llegar have a u: llegue?
choices: To keep the g sounding hard before e
Because llegar is a stem-changing verb
To make the word easier to say
check.why: G before e would sound soft, like j. The silent u keeps the hard g sound from the infinitive, exactly as in the preterite llegué.

lessons.title: The Six Irregulars
lessons.mainIdea: Six common verbs do not follow the yo-form rule in the present subjunctive: sea, esté, vaya, haya, sepa and dé.
reading: The yo-form rule covers almost every verb in Spanish, because it is really a rule about the stem. But six verbs have yo forms that give no usable stem. *Ser* (to be) has soy. *Estar* (to be) has estoy. *Ir* (to go) has voy. *Haber* (there is, there are) has hay, and its true yo form is he. *Saber* (to know a fact) has sé. *Dar* (to give) has doy. Drop the -o from soy or doy and nothing helpful is left. So these six use special stems.

Here they are. Ser: sea, seas, sea, seamos, seáis, sean. Estar: esté, estés, esté, estemos, estéis, estén. Ir: vaya, vayas, vaya, vayamos, vayáis, vayan. Haber: haya (used mostly as the there-is form, "Espero que haya tiempo," I hope there is time). Saber: sepa, sepas, sepa, sepamos, sepáis, sepan. Dar: dé, des, dé, demos, deis, den. Two of these carry accents for a reason. *Esté* is stressed on the last syllable, so it needs the mark. *Dé* takes an accent to look different from de (of), even though both are one syllable.

You have already met these six as the stems of the usted commands: sea, esté, vaya, sepa, dé, plus haya. The command and the subjunctive are the same form, which is one reason the subjunctive feels familiar to heritage speakers. Lucía's letter uses two of them: "Espero que mamá esté bien" (I hope Mom is well) and "Ojalá que vayas a la biblioteca" (I hope you go to the library). A grandparent's "Que Dios te dé salud" (May God give you health) uses a third.

A memory trick many students use is the first letters: sea, esté, vaya, haya, sepa, dé. Learn them as a set, say them aloud until they come without effort, and watch for the two accents. The most common mistake is writing este for esté, which turns I hope she is into this.

words.d: to be (identity, traits) — irregular subjunctive: sea, seas, sea, seamos, seáis, sean
to be (location, condition) — irregular subjunctive: esté, estés, esté, estemos, estéis, estén
to go — irregular subjunctive: vaya, vayas, vaya, vayamos, vayáis, vayan
to have (helper verb); hay = there is — subjunctive haya: Espero que haya tiempo (I hope there is time)
to know a fact or how to — irregular subjunctive: sepa, sepas, sepa, sepamos, sepáis, sepan
to give — irregular subjunctive: dé, des, dé, demos, deis, den

look.title: A Blessing at the Door
look.text: Before Lucía left in August, her grandmother stood at the door and said: Que Dios te dé salud. Que estés bien. Que no vayas sola de noche. Que sepas que te queremos. Que seas feliz. (May God give you health. May you be well. May you not go out alone at night. May you know that we love you. May you be happy.) Each line begins with que and a wish, so each verb is subjunctive.
look.prompt: Find all five irregular forms in the blessing and match each to its infinitive. Which one is missing from the set of six?

check.q: Which form belongs to ser in the subjunctive?
check.why: Ser becomes sea, seas, sea. Sé is the yo form of saber, soy is the indicative of ser, and sabe is indicative of saber.

check.q: Espero que ___ (haber) suficiente comida para todos.
check.why: Haber's there-is form in the subjunctive is haya: Espero que haya (I hope there is). Hay is the indicative.

check.q: Why does dé carry an accent mark?
choices: Because it is stressed on the second syllable
Because all subjunctive forms take accents
Because it is a question word
To tell it apart from the preposition de
check.why: Dé and de sound the same. The accent marks the verb form (give) so it is not confused with de (of, from).

lessons.title: Wishes and Wants
lessons.mainIdea: Verbs of wanting, hoping and needing, such as querer, esperar, desear and necesitar, trigger the subjunctive when a que clause has a new subject.
reading: Teachers often use the letters WEIRDO to remember what triggers the subjunctive: Wishes, Emotions, Impersonal expressions, Recommendations, Doubt, and Ojalá. This lesson takes the W. A wish is any verb that expresses what the speaker wants to happen, especially when another person has to do it. *Querer que* (to want that), *esperar que* (to hope that), *desear que* (to wish that), *necesitar que* (to need that), and *preferir que* (to prefer that) all belong here.

Watch the pattern in Lucía's own words. "Quiero que estudies un poco cada día." Querer, que, new subject, subjunctive. "Espero que mamá esté bien." Esperar, que, new subject, subjunctive. "Necesito que me llames el domingo" (I need you to call me on Sunday). Necesitar, que, new subject, subjunctive. Every one of these sentences describes something that has not happened yet and may not happen. Lucía cannot make Mateo study. She can only want it. The subjunctive marks that gap between wanting and being.

Now the contrast that catches English speakers. "I want to study" and "I want you to study" look almost the same in English. In Spanish they are built differently. "Quiero estudiar" keeps one subject and uses the infinitive. "Quiero que estudies" has two subjects and needs que plus the subjunctive. The mistake to avoid is dragging the English pattern across: "Quiero tú estudiar" and "Quiero que estudias" are both wrong, one for word order and one for mood.

A short set of examples you can copy. Mis padres quieren que yo vaya a la universidad (My parents want me to go to college). Prefiero que tú manejes (I prefer that you drive). Esperamos que ustedes vengan a la fiesta (We hope you come to the party). Deseo que tengas un buen día (I wish you a good day). Notice that the subjunctive verb is always the second one, never the verb of wanting itself.

words.d: to want (someone) to — a wish trigger: Quiero que estudies (I want you to study)
to hope that — a wish trigger: Espero que vengas (I hope you come)
to need (someone) to — a wish trigger: Necesito que me ayudes (I need you to help me)
to prefer that — a wish trigger: Prefiero que tú manejes (I prefer that you drive)

look.title: Family Wishes
look.text: At Sunday dinner, everyone has a wish for Mateo. Mamá: Quiero que comas más verduras. Papá: Espero que saques buenas notas este semestre. Abuela: Necesito que me acompañes a la iglesia. Lucía, on the phone: Prefiero que no trabajes tantas horas. Mateo: Y yo quiero que todos me dejen en paz un ratito. (And I want everyone to leave me alone for a little while.)
look.prompt: Underline the trigger, the que, and the subjunctive verb in each sentence. Then write one wish your family has for you, in Spanish.

check.q: Mis padres quieren que yo ___ (ir) a la universidad.
check.why: Querer que with a new subject (my parents want, I go) takes the subjunctive of ir: vaya.

check.q: Which sentence is wrong?
check.why: After querer que with a new subject, the verb must be subjunctive: vengas, not vienes. The other three are correct.

check.q: In "Deseo que tengas un buen día," which verb is in the subjunctive?
check.why: The trigger verb deseo stays indicative. The verb after que, tengas, is the subjunctive form of tener.

lessons.title: Emotions and Impersonal Expressions
lessons.mainIdea: Reactions such as me alegra que and me molesta que, and judgments such as es importante que and es necesario que, trigger the subjunctive in the que clause.
reading: The E in WEIRDO stands for emotions. When the main clause reports a feeling about something someone else does, the que clause takes the subjunctive. *Me alegra que* (I am glad that), *me molesta que* (it bothers me that), *me sorprende que* (it surprises me that), *siento que* (I am sorry that), *temo que* (I fear that). "Me alegra que Lucía esté contenta" (I am glad Lucía is happy). Lucía's happiness may be a fact, but the sentence is about my reaction to it, and Spanish marks that with the mood.

The I stands for impersonal expressions. These begin with es (it is) plus an adjective and are called impersonal because no person is the subject. *Es importante que* (it is important that), *es necesario que* (it is necessary that), *es bueno que* (it is good that), *es mejor que* (it is better that), *es posible que* (it is possible that), *es una lástima que* (it is a shame that). Lucía wrote "Es importante que duermas." She is not reporting that Mateo sleeps; she is judging that sleeping matters.

A useful test: does the main clause tell you what is true, or how someone feels or judges? "Es verdad que Lucía estudia mucho" (It is true that Lucía studies a lot) states a fact, so the verb stays indicative. "Es bueno que Lucía estudie mucho" (It is good that Lucía studies a lot) judges, so the verb turns subjunctive. Es verdad que, es cierto que, es obvio que and es evidente que all report certainty and keep the indicative. Almost every other es plus adjective phrase triggers the subjunctive.

When there is no specific subject, the impersonal expression takes an infinitive: "Es importante dormir" (It is important to sleep). Add a subject and you need que and the subjunctive: "Es importante que tú duermas." That is the same one-subject-or-two logic from earlier in the chapter.

words.d: I am glad that — an emotion trigger: Me alegra que estés aquí (I am glad you are here)
it bothers me that — an emotion trigger: Me molesta que lleguen tarde (It bothers me that they arrive late)
it is important that — an impersonal trigger: Es importante que duermas (It is important that you sleep)
it is a shame that — an impersonal trigger: Es una lástima que no vengas (It is a shame you are not coming)
it is true that — reports a fact, so it keeps the indicative: Es verdad que estudia mucho

look.cite: A made-up budget Lucía sends home, for practice only
look.prompt: Write two reactions in Spanish, one with me sorprende que and one with es necesario que, about any of these numbers. Check that both verbs after que are subjunctive.

check.q: Me alegra que tú ___ (estar) contento con tus clases.
check.why: Me alegra que expresses an emotion about someone else, so the verb is the subjunctive estés. Estás is indicative.

check.q: Which expression keeps the indicative in the que clause?
check.why: Es verdad que reports a fact: Es verdad que estudia. The other three judge or react, which triggers the subjunctive.

check.q: What does "Es una lástima que no puedas venir" mean?
choices: It is true that you cannot come.
It is a shame that you cannot come.
It is a shame that I cannot come.
It is lucky that you can come.
check.why: Es una lástima que means it is a shame that, and puedas is the tú subjunctive of poder, so the person who cannot come is you.

lessons.title: Recommendations and Requests
lessons.mainIdea: Verbs of advising, asking and telling, such as recomendar, sugerir, pedir and decir, trigger the subjunctive when someone is told what to do.
reading: The R in WEIRDO is for recommendations, which also covers requests and softened commands. *Recomendar que* (to recommend that), *sugerir que* (to suggest that), *aconsejar que* (to advise that), *pedir que* (to ask that), *insistir en que* (to insist that), and *decir que* when it means to tell someone to do something. Lucía wrote "Te recomiendo que hables con tus maestros." Recommend, que, you talk, subjunctive. The advice is a hope dressed as a tip.

Many of these verbs take an indirect object pronoun in front: *te recomiendo* (I recommend to you), *le pido* (I ask him or her), *les sugiero* (I suggest to them). The pronoun tells you who receives the advice, and the que clause tells you what they should do. "Le pido a mi hermano que me escriba" (I ask my brother to write to me). "Les aconsejo que lleguen temprano" (I advise them to arrive early). Do not let the pronoun fool you into thinking it is the subject; the subject of the subjunctive verb is the person who will act.

*Decir* is the tricky one, because it lives in two moods. When decir reports information, the que clause is indicative: "Lucía dice que la comida es buena" (Lucía says the food is good). When decir gives an order, the que clause is subjunctive: "Lucía dice que comas bien" (Lucía says to eat well, or Lucía tells you to eat well). The same is true of *insistir*. Ask whether the sentence passes on a fact or presses someone to act, and the mood will follow.

One more piece of good news. The usted and ustedes commands you already know, hable, coma, vaya, are the same forms as the subjunctive. "Hable con el maestro" (Talk to the teacher) and "Le recomiendo que hable con el maestro" (I recommend that you talk to the teacher) use the same word. Recommendations are polite commands with a que in front.

words.d: to recommend that — e→ie: Te recomiendo que hables con tus maestros (I recommend that you talk with your teachers)
to suggest that — e→ie: Les sugiero que lleguen temprano (I suggest that you all arrive early)
to ask (someone) to — e→i: Le pido que me escriba (I ask him or her to write to me)
to advise that — Te aconsejo que duermas (I advise you to sleep)
to say that (indicative) or to tell someone to (subjunctive): Dice que come bien / Dice que comas bien

look.title: Advice for the First Week
look.text: Lucía's list for Mateo, who will visit campus in November. Te recomiendo que traigas una chaqueta; hace frío en noviembre. Te sugiero que llegues antes del mediodía. Te pido que no le digas a mamá que comemos pizza todas las noches. Te aconsejo que conozcas a mis amigos; son muy simpáticos. (I recommend that you bring a jacket; it is cold in November. I suggest that you arrive before noon. I ask you not to tell Mom that we eat pizza every night. I advise you to meet my friends; they are very nice.)
look.prompt: Which sentence uses a verb with a yo-form stem (g or zc) in the subjunctive? Which one has a spelling change? Write one more piece of advice with te recomiendo que.

check.q: Te recomiendo que ___ (hablar) con la consejera.
check.why: Recomendar que triggers the subjunctive, and the person who will talk is tú: hables.

check.q: Which sentence means "Lucía tells you to eat well"?
check.why: Decir with a subjunctive clause gives an order: dice que comas. With the indicative comes, it only reports that you eat well.

check.q: In "Le pido a mi hermano que me escriba," who will do the writing?
check.why: Le and a mi hermano name the person asked. He is the subject of escriba, the subjunctive of escribir.

lessons.title: Doubt and Ojalá
lessons.mainIdea: Expressions of doubt or denial, and the word ojalá, trigger the subjunctive; expressions of belief and certainty keep the indicative.
reading: The D in WEIRDO is doubt. *Dudar que* (to doubt that), *no creer que* (to not believe that), *no estar seguro de que* (to not be sure that), *no es cierto que* (it is not true that), *negar que* (to deny that). "Dudo que Mateo estudie todos los días" (I doubt Mateo studies every day). The speaker is not reporting what Mateo does. The speaker is holding the idea at a distance, and the subjunctive marks that distance.

The flip side matters just as much. *Creer que* (to believe that), *pensar que* (to think that), *estar seguro de que* (to be sure that), *es cierto que* (it is true that) express confidence, so their que clause stays indicative. "Creo que Mateo estudia todos los días" (I think Mateo studies every day). The only change between creo que estudia and no creo que estudie is the word no, and it flips the mood. This is one of the clearest places in Spanish where the mood carries meaning by itself.

The O in WEIRDO is *ojalá*, a word Spanish took from Arabic during the centuries when Arabic was spoken across much of the Iberian Peninsula. It comes from a phrase meaning if God wills, and today it means I hope or let's hope. Ojalá is always followed by the subjunctive, with or without que. "Ojalá que vengas en noviembre" (I hope you come in November). "Ojalá llueva" (I hope it rains). It has no subject and no conjugation; it simply opens the door to a wish.

Two habits to build. First, when you hear no in front of creer, pensar or es cierto, switch to the subjunctive. Second, when you hear ojalá, do not look for a trigger verb; ojalá is the trigger. "Ojalá que mamá no trabaje tanto" is a complete, correct sentence, and it is exactly what Lucía wrote.

words.d: to doubt that — a doubt trigger: Dudo que estudie (I doubt he studies)
to not believe that — doubt, subjunctive: No creo que venga (I do not think she is coming)
to believe that — confidence, indicative: Creo que viene (I think she is coming)
I hope, let's hope — from Arabic, always followed by the subjunctive: Ojalá que llueva (I hope it rains)
to deny that — e→ie, a doubt trigger: Niega que sea difícil (He denies that it is hard)

look.title: A Proverb with a Hidden Subjunctive
look.text: No hay mal que por bien no venga. (There is no bad thing that does not come for some good.) The last verb is venga, the subjunctive of venir. The proverb is talking about a bad thing that may or may not exist, not a specific one, and Spanish uses the subjunctive for what is uncertain or unknown.
look.cite: Traditional Spanish proverb, centuries old, author unknown
look.prompt: Why is venga subjunctive here instead of viene? What English saying carries the same idea?

check.q: No creo que Lucía ___ (tener) tiempo para llamar hoy.
check.why: No creer que expresses doubt, so the verb is subjunctive: tenga. Creo que tiene, without no, would be indicative.

check.q: Which sentence is correct?
check.why: Ojalá is always followed by the subjunctive: vengas. Vienes is indicative and the infinitive does not fit.

check.q: What changes the mood between "Creo que estudia" and "No creo que estudie"?
choices: The tense changes to the future
The word no turns belief into doubt
check.why: Creer que shows confidence and takes the indicative. No creer que shows doubt and takes the subjunctive.

lessons.title: When Not to Use It
lessons.mainIdea: No change of subject means an infinitive, and a main clause that reports or believes means the indicative; the subjunctive is only for a que clause that wishes, doubts or reacts about a different subject.
reading: Once students learn the subjunctive, many start using it everywhere, so this lesson is about restraint. Rule one: no change of subject, no subjunctive. "Quiero ir" (I want to go), "Espero terminar" (I hope to finish), "Prefiero manejar" (I prefer to drive). One person wants and does, so the second verb is an infinitive. Writing "Quiero que yo vaya" is a common learner error; it is grammatical but unnatural, like saying I want that I go.

Rule two: reporting and believing take the indicative. "Sé que Lucía estudia" (I know Lucía studies). "Creo que la comida es buena" (I think the food is good). "Es cierto que hace frío" (It is true that it is cold). "Lucía dice que tiene mucha tarea" (Lucía says she has a lot of homework). Each main clause treats the que clause as a fact. Learners who have just memorized WEIRDO sometimes write "Sé que Lucía estudie." Saber, creer without no, es verdad and decir when it reports are not triggers.

Rule three: the trigger verb itself is never subjunctive. In "Quiero que vengas," only vengas changes. Writing "Quiera que vengas" is a mistake that comes from over-applying the endings. The main clause stays in whatever indicative tense fits, and only the verb after que takes the new mood. A quick check is to cover everything before que; the remaining verb is the only candidate.

Put the three rules together as questions. Is there a que with a new subject? If not, use an infinitive. Does the main clause wish, feel, judge, advise or doubt? If not, use the indicative. If both answers are yes, use the subjunctive, and only on the second verb. Mateo runs each of Lucía's sentences through those questions and every one comes out right.

words.d: to know that — reports a fact, indicative: Sé que estudias (I know you study)
it is true that — certainty, indicative: Es cierto que hace frío (It is true that it is cold)
to think that — confidence, indicative: Pienso que tienes razón (I think you are right)
the main verb — the trigger verb before que, which stays in the indicative: Quiero que vengas

look.title: Sort the Sentences
look.text: Six sentences from Mateo's reply. 1. Sé que tienes mucha tarea. 2. Quiero visitarte en noviembre. 3. Espero que no llueva ese fin de semana. 4. Es cierto que mamá trabaja mucho. 5. Ojalá que ella descanse pronto. 6. Prefiero tomar el tren. Three use the indicative or infinitive and three use the subjunctive.
look.prompt: Sort them into two groups and name the reason for each: no change of subject, a fact reported, or a wish about another subject.

check.q: Which sentence should use the infinitive?
check.why: Espero terminar has one subject: I hope, I finish. No que, no change of subject, so the infinitive is right.

check.q: Sé que mi hermana ___ (estudiar) mucho.
check.why: Saber que reports a fact and keeps the indicative: estudia. Estudie would wrongly treat a known fact as a wish or doubt.

check.q: Which sentence has an error in the main verb?
check.why: The trigger verb stays indicative: quiero, not quiera. Only the verb after que takes the subjunctive.

lessons.title: Writing Back to Lucía
lessons.mainIdea: A letter of advice combines wishes, emotions, recommendations and hopes, each one built as main clause, que, new subject, subjunctive.
reading: Mateo's reply puts the whole chapter on one page. He opens with an emotion: "Me alegra que estés contenta en la universidad" (I am glad you are happy at college). Emotion trigger, que, new subject, subjunctive of estar. He follows with a wish: "Espero que tus clases no sean muy difíciles" (I hope your classes are not very hard). Then an impersonal judgment: "Es bueno que tengas amigos nuevos" (It is good that you have new friends). Three sentences, three triggers, three subjunctive verbs, and every one was chosen on purpose.

Then he gives advice back, which is the fun part. "Te recomiendo que llames a la abuela los domingos; ella te extraña" (I recommend that you call Grandma on Sundays; she misses you). "Te sugiero que no comas pizza todas las noches" (I suggest that you not eat pizza every night). "Mamá dice que duermas más" (Mom says to sleep more). Notice that decir here is giving an instruction, so duermas is subjunctive, and dormir keeps its stem change in the tú form.

He closes with doubt and hope. "No creo que pueda visitarte en noviembre porque tengo un torneo" (I do not think I can visit you in November because I have a tournament). Poder becomes pueda. "Pero ojalá que vengas a casa para el Día de Acción de Gracias" (But I hope you come home for Thanksgiving). Then the one-subject sentences that need no subjunctive at all: "Quiero verte pronto" (I want to see you soon) and "Sé que estás muy ocupada" (I know you are very busy).

A letter like this is a checklist in disguise. Wishes, emotions, impersonal expressions, recommendations, doubt, ojalá: each one appears, each one takes que and a new subject, and each one ends in the opposite vowel. When you write your own letter at the end of this unit, use Mateo's as a map, and read every subjunctive verb aloud with its trigger to hear whether it fits.

words.d: to miss (a person) — Ella te extraña (She misses you); indicative, because it reports a feeling as a fact

words.w: el Día de Acción de Gracias
words.d: Thanksgiving Day — Ojalá que vengas para el Día de Acción de Gracias (I hope you come for Thanksgiving)
to be able to — o→ue in the subjunctive: pueda, puedas, pueda, podamos, podáis, puedan
letter of advice — a letter built from wishes, emotions and recommendations in the subjunctive

No creo que pueda visitarte en noviembre, pero ojalá que vengas a casa en diciembre. Quiero verte pronto. Sé que estás muy ocupada. Un abrazo, Mateo.

check.why: Me alegra que is an emotion trigger with a new subject, so the verb is the subjunctive estés.

check.why: When decir tells someone to do something, the que clause is subjunctive: duermas. Duermes only reports that you sleep more.

choices: Because the sentence is in the future
Because the same person wants and sees, so there is no change of subject

review.q: Which sentence is in the subjunctive mood?
review.why: Querer que with a new subject triggers the subjunctive estudie. The other three are indicative in the present, preterite and near future.

review.why: Ir is one of the six irregulars: vaya, vayas, vaya. Vas is indicative, ves is from ver, and irás is future.

review.q: Which of these does NOT trigger the subjunctive?
review.why: Es verdad que reports certainty and keeps the indicative. The others express judgment, hope and doubt.

review.q: Which sentence is correct Spanish for "I want to sleep"?
review.why: With no change of subject, Spanish uses the infinitive: Quiero dormir. Quiero que yo duerma is unnatural, and the others are not grammatical.

review.q: Quiero que tú ___ (empezar) la tarea ahora.
review.why: Empezar keeps its e→ie change in tú and changes z to c before e: empieces. Empiezas is indicative; the others have spelling errors.

review.q: What does "No creo que mi hermana tenga tiempo" mean?

I do not think my sister has time.
My sister does not have time.
I hope my sister has time.
